# AI Disclosure Law

> Dated, source-linked reference on US state AI disclosure and transparency obligations. Every page states a verification date and links the enrolled bill text. Independent reference; not legal advice.

Core facts as of 2026-11-09:
- Six states have enforceable AI disclosure or transparency duties: California, Texas, Illinois, Utah, Maine, New York.
- Colorado's SB 26-189 takes effect January 1, 2027. The 2024 Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205) never became operative and was repealed on May 14, 2026.
- California AB 2839 is permanently enjoined (Kohls v. Bonta, Aug 29 2025) and AB 2655 is preempted by Section 230. Neither is enforceable.
- California SB 942 applies only to generative AI providers with more than 1,000,000 monthly California users.
- Texas TRAIGA imposes a disclosure duty on government entities and health care providers only, not on private companies generally.

## Pages

- [About This Site: How Every Page Is Verified](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/about/): AI Disclosure Law is an independent reference on US state AI disclosure and transparency obligations. Every page is built from the enrolled bill text, links its official sources, states the date it was last verified, and gets updated when a statute is amended, a date moves, or a court bars enforcement.
- [California AI Law: Four Narrow Laws, No General Rule](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/california/): California is the most-legislated and least-imposing AI state at once: three narrow, provider-side statutes are in force — SB 942, SB 53, and AB 2013 — none of which puts a disclosure duty on an ordinary business that merely uses AI. Two headline election-AI laws are unenforceable after federal court rulings, and the one election rule that survives predates all of them.
- [California AB 2013: Training Data Disclosure Requirements](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/california/ab-2013/): Since January 1, 2026, developers of publicly available generative AI systems must post a high-level summary of their training data on their website — sources, ownership, volume, whether it includes copyrighted or personal information, and whether synthetic data was used. The statute specifies no penalty and no enforcement agency.
- [Is California's AB 2839 Still Enforceable? No — Here Is What Still Applies](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/california/ab-2839/): AB 2839 was permanently enjoined in August 2025 as a First Amendment violation, and California did not appeal that ruling. AB 2655 was held preempted by Section 230 and is barred against every interactive computer service. The election-AI rule California can still enforce is Elections Code §20010.
- [California SB 53: Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/california/sb-53/): Since January 1, 2026, anyone training a model above 10^26 FLOPs must publish a transparency report before release and report critical safety incidents to Cal OES within 15 days. Large frontier developers — over $500 million in revenue — must also publish a safety framework and face up to $1 million per violation.
- [California AI Transparency Act (SB 942 + AB 853): Who It Actually Covers](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/california/sb-942/): SB 942 requires generative AI providers with more than 1 million monthly users in California to embed provenance data in AI-generated images, video, and audio, and to offer a free public detection tool. The core duties took effect August 2, 2026 — and they do not apply to most businesses that merely use AI.
- [Colorado AI Law: What Is Actually in Effect in 2026](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/colorado/): Colorado's original AI Act never took effect. SB 24-205 was repealed and replaced on May 14, 2026, a month before its own start date. The law that applies to you is the Automated Decision-Making Technology Act (SB 26-189), and its duties begin January 1, 2027.
- [Colorado SB 26-189: The Automated Decision-Making Technology Act](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/colorado/sb-26-189/): From January 1, 2027, if you use automated decision-making technology that materially influences a consequential decision about a Colorado resident, you must tell them before you use it and, within 30 days of an adverse outcome, explain what the technology did and how they can get a human to review it.
- [Colorado vs Texas AI Law: Disclosure Obligations Compared](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/compare/colorado-vs-texas/): Colorado requires every developer and deployer of automated decision-making technology to give pre-use notice and post-decision explanations, starting January 1, 2027. Texas requires disclosure only from government agencies and health care providers, and has been in force since January 1, 2026. If you operate in both states, Colorado is the binding constraint.
- [Illinois AI Law: Two Statutes, One Missing Rulebook](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/illinois/): Illinois regulates AI in the workplace through two statutes: HB 3773 (Public Act 103-0804), in force since January 1, 2026, which makes failing to notify employees of AI use in employment decisions a civil rights violation with no damage-proof requirement, and the older Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act (AIVIA, 820 ILCS 42). The rules that were supposed to define a compliant notice were withdrawn on June 2, 2026 and have not been refiled.
- [Illinois AI Law (HB 3773): The AI Notice Duty With No Rules Behind It](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/illinois/hb-3773/): Since January 1, 2026, Illinois has treated two things as separate civil rights violations: using AI in a way that discriminates in employment, and using AI in an employment decision without telling people. The notice duty does not depend on proving any discriminatory effect — you either told them or you did not. And the rules that were supposed to define what a compliant notice looks like were withdrawn on June 2, 2026 and have not been refiled.
- [Which State AI Disclosure Laws Are in Effect Right Now](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/in-effect/): As of November 8, 2026, six states have AI disclosure or transparency duties that can be enforced today: California, Texas, Illinois, Utah, Maine, and New York. Colorado's duties start January 1, 2027. Two California election laws are barred by court order.
- [Maine AI Law: No Threshold, No Intent, No Excuses](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/maine/): Maine's AI law, 10 M.R.S. §1500-DD (in force since September 24, 2025), bars using an AI chatbot — or any other computer technology — to engage in trade or commerce in a way that may mislead a reasonable consumer into thinking they are dealing with a human, unless the consumer is clearly and conspicuously notified otherwise. No employee threshold, no revenue test, no intent element. A violation is a Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act violation. A separate synthetic-media rule for political ads lives at 21-A §1014(5-C), in force July 29, 2026.
- [Maine's Chatbot Disclosure Law: No Threshold, No Intent, No Excuses](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/maine/chatbot-disclosure/): 10 M.R.S. §1500-DD has been in force since September 24, 2025 and is the strictest chatbot disclosure rule in the country: no company-size threshold, no intent requirement, no carve-out for a bot that tries hard. If a reasonable consumer could be misled into thinking they are talking to a person, you owe a clear and conspicuous notice — and the section number is not the one most articles still print.
- [New York AI Law: The First Synthetic Performer Disclosure Rule](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/new-york/): New York's AI law for advertising (S8420-A, amending General Business Law §296-b) took effect June 9, 2026: any visual or audiovisual ad distributed to a New York consumer that features an AI-generated human who is not an identifiable real person needs a conspicuous disclosure. Penalties are $1,000 for a first violation and $5,000 after, enforced by the Attorney General. A companion law expanded the post-mortem right of publicity for digital replicas of identifiable people.
- [New York Requires Ads to Disclose AI-Generated Humans](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/new-york/synthetic-performer/): Since June 9, 2026, a visual or audiovisual advertisement distributed to a New York audience that features an AI-generated human has to carry a conspicuous disclosure that the person is not real. It is the first state law of its kind, it reaches advertisers anywhere in the world whose ads reach New York, and the exposure is not the brand campaign — it is the product listing with an AI model holding the product.
- [Texas AI Law: TRAIGA, in Force Since January 1, 2026](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/texas/): Texas's AI law is the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA, HB 149), in force since January 1, 2026. Its affirmative disclosure duties fall on government entities and health care providers only — private companies face a prohibition list instead, every prohibition requires intent, and enforcement is exclusively the Attorney General's.
- [Texas AI Law (TRAIGA, HB 149): Who Actually Has to Disclose AI](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/texas/traiga/): Since January 1, 2026, Texas requires government agencies to disclose AI before or at the moment a consumer interacts with it, and health care providers to disclose by the date service is first provided. Private companies have no general AI disclosure duty under TRAIGA — they face its prohibitions instead.
- [Utah's AI Disclosure Law Now Lives in Code Chapter 77](https://aidisclosurelaw.com/utah/): If you are citing Utah Code §13-2-12 for the state's AI disclosure duty, you are citing a section that was repealed in 2025. The live rule is Title 13, Chapter 77, in force since May 7, 2025. It splits into a reactive duty (disclose when a consumer clearly asks) and a proactive one (regulated occupations, high-risk interactions), and it hands you a safe harbour that is easier to test than either.
